title: The second council
hookLine: a hundred years after the Buddha, at Vesali, a dispute over ten points, including handling money (Vinaya, Cullavagga 12)

lines: A BOWL OF WATER, A CITY.
cards: A bronze bowl full of water sits in the middle of the gathered monks. It's the observance day in the city of Vesali, and lay people are coming in. The monks ask them to drop coins into the bowl for the community.
A visiting monk named Yasa watches this and can't stay quiet. Don't give, he tells the lay people. Gold and silver aren't allowed to monks.
The Vinaya says this happened a hundred years after the Buddha's death.

teach.b: The monks of Vesali don't take Yasa's protest well. They tell him he has insulted the lay people and must go and apologize. He goes, but instead of apologizing, he explains why the Buddha forbade monks to take money.
The lay people are persuaded, and they side with him. Now the Vesali monks want him out.
Yasa travels to find senior monks, and it turns out the coins are only one of ten practices the Vesali monks have allowed themselves.

Most of them sound tiny: carrying salt in a horn so food can be salted later; eating when the sun's shadow has moved two fingers past noon; drinking palm juice that hasn't quite turned to wine; a sitting rug without a fringe.
Small loosenings, each one with an argument behind it. Senior monks gather at Vesali.
To keep the meeting from turning into a shouting match, they hand the questions to a small panel drawn from both sides.

teach.h: TEN SMALL BENDS, ONE BY ONE.
teach.b: The panel goes through the ten points one at a time, checking each against the rules, and finds every one of them not allowed. In this account, a hundred years in, the hard questions weren't about grand doctrine.
They were about salt, sunlight and coins. The elders had promised to keep every rule.
Here is what keeping that promise looked like: not a single dramatic heresy, but ten small bends, each one easy to explain, examined one by one.

how: Under the Theravada monastic code, monks are not to accept gold and silver, and lay stewards may look after money given for a monastery.

o: the monk who objected to taking coins
the monk who led the Vesali community
a lay donor who filled the bronze bowl

s: the second council argued over big questions of doctrine
the ten points were small practices: salt, mealtimes, palm juice, a rug, and taking money.
the dispute began with coins in a bowl of water
monks at Vesali asked lay people to drop coins in it for the community, and Yasa objected.
Yasa apologized to the lay people as he was told
he went to them and explained instead why monks may not take gold and silver.

games.q: you're Yasa. the local monks say you insulted the lay people by telling them not to give coins, and must apologize. what do you do?
o: go to the lay people and explain the rule instead.
games.why: he explains why the Buddha forbade monks to take money, and the lay people side with him. that is what pushes the dispute to the elders.

practice: Think of one small rule you made for yourself or agreed to, a bedtime, a budget, a promise about your phone, and find where you've let it slide a little.
Don't scold; just hear the reason you give yourself clearly, the way the elders heard each point.

wordCard.voice: Yasa. The visiting monk who objected to coins in the alms bowl, and set off the dispute that led to this council. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the ten points. Each bend came with a reason that sounded fine. That's day eight hundred fifty-four.
